deep.reconstruction:
This page is not Euler's mathematics proper. It is part of the editorial summary that precedes E296 in Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 10 (for 1764, printed 1766). The summary is written in the third person ('Auctor').

The page sets out the general isoperimetric problem in purely analytic form. V is an arbitrary expression built from two variables x and y, their differentials of any order, and even integral formulas. One seeks the relation y(x) that makes the functional J[y] = ∫V dx a maximum or minimum. In modern terms this is the extremization of a functional whose Lagrangian may contain higher derivatives y', y'', ... and nonlocal terms of the form ∫W dx. Higher derivatives lead to the Euler–Poisson equation; the nonlocal terms are the 'integral formulas' Euler had treated in the Methodus inveniendi (1744).

The text makes four points.
1. Once the problem is posed this way it is completely separated from geometry, so the 'genuine' method of solving it should also be free of geometry.
2. Euler had long sought such a method and had told friends of the wish. The glory of first discovery went to Lagrange of Turin, who by analysis alone obtained exactly the solution Euler had derived from geometric considerations about the elements of the curve, i.e. polygonal approximation.
3. Lagrange's solution seemed to constitute a new species of analysis. This gave Euler the occasion to enrich the subject with a new kind of calculus, which he calls 'Calculus variationum'; E296 sets out its elements.
4. The contrast with the differential calculus: both concern infinitely small increments. The differential calculus derives, from a given relation between variables, the relation among their differentials of every order. The calculus of variations, as the next page explains, instead lets the relation itself change infinitely little, y → y + δy. Euler writes δ for this to distinguish it from d.

In modern language this is the distinction between the differential of a function along its graph and the first variation of a functional under a perturbation of the function. The page states the motivating problem and the history; it contains no derivation.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. Historically, 'eandem plane solutionem' is broadly right: Lagrange's δ-method (letter to Euler, 1755; Miscellanea Taurinensia 2, 1762) reproduced the Euler equations of the Methodus inveniendi. Lagrange's method also yields the boundary (transversality) terms, as the following page hints ('pleniores ac perfectiores solutiones'). The name 'calculus of variations' itself first appeared in print in Euler's E296.

ideas.what: Formulation of the extremum problem for ∫V dx, with V depending on x, y, derivatives of any order and integral formulas, as a purely analytic problem detached from geometry
ideas.modern_name: General variational problem with higher-order and nonlocal Lagrangians (Euler–Poisson equation, isoperimetric/integral constraints)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744); E296; E297

ideas.what: Credit to Lagrange for the first purely analytic (δ) method; Euler names it 'calculus variationum'
ideas.modern_name: Origin of the calculus of variations and of the δ-notation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755 letter, 1762 paper); name by Euler (E296, 1766)
ideas.where_published: E296/E297; Euler–Lagrange correspondence; standard histories (Goldstine, Fraser, Opera omnia I.25 introduction by Carathéodory)

ideas.what: Conceptual contrast between differential calculus (relation fixed, differentials sought) and variational calculus (the relation itself perturbed by δy)
ideas.modern_name: Differential vs. first variation of a functional
ideas.where_published: E296 itself and its summary; later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 3 appendix (E385)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editorial summary recounting the well-documented story of Lagrange's priority and Euler's naming of the calculus of variations. It is thoroughly covered in the standard historiography.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. The page number is printed as '12'. The image shows a stray mark after 'y' in 'x, y, earumque', which is a printing artifact, not a symbol. In the original the long s (ſ) is used throughout, as in the neighbouring transcriptions ('Quaeſtio', 'propoſita', etc.).
